issues.description: HAS_NAMED and HAS_PERCENTAGE keyword regexes built without escaping risk silent miscompilation
issues.detail: The new regexes interpolate keyword sets directly into RegExp source. Today these tokens are alphanumerics and hyphens, so it works; but the construction complects 'list of keywords' (data) with 'regex pattern' (code) without escaping. A future addition to fontWeightNonNumericKeywords or PERCENTAGE_SELECTORS containing a regex metachar will produce a wrong-but-valid regex. Pass the keywords through an escape helper, or assert it at module load.

issues.description: import-notation prefilter complects lexical url( detection with the rule's actual semantics
issues.detail: `/url\(/i.test(params)` treats any substring 'url(' as a url() function, including inside strings or comments. The rule itself later uses valueParser to make that distinction properly. Two different notions of 'has url()' now coexist; the cheap one gates the careful one. If they ever disagree on edge cases (url inside a string, escaped paren), the rule silently stops firing. The prefilter should match what the parser would conclude, or be scoped narrowly enough that it cannot.

issues.description: Per-rule prefilter regexes are an incidental pattern that wants to be one named helper
issues.detail: Five rules now grow the same shape: build a keyword-set regex at module top, then bail early in the walk callback. The pattern is essentially 'cheap value predicate before expensive parse.' Right now it is open-coded five different ways with subtly different word boundaries and flags. A single small helper that takes a keyword list and returns a predicate would make the value (what counts as 'has this token') explicit and reusable, instead of incidental to each rule.

issues.description: selectorRegex `/./` sentinel in keyframe-selector-notation conflates 'no filter' with 'filter that matches everything'
issues.detail: When primary is 'percentage-unless-within-keyword-only-block', the code sets `selectorRegex = /./` so walkRules still receives a filter. This works but braids two concerns: 'should we filter?' and 'what is the filter?'. A clearer shape is to branch on whether to pass a filter at all, or to compute the selectorsInBlock list and pass undefined. The sentinel reads as a hack to satisfy a single API signature.

issues.description: HAS_PERCENTAGE uses different word-boundary logic than HAS_KEYWORD without stated reason
issues.detail: HAS_PERCENTAGE uses `(?:^|[,\s])` while HAS_KEYWORD uses `\b`, and only the keyword regex is case-insensitive. The asymmetry may be intentional (percent signs are not word chars; from/to are case-insensitive identifiers), but it is not documented. A short comment naming why the two prefilters differ would keep a future reader from 'fixing' one to match the other.

review.summary: The change is a sensible cheap-predicate-before-expensive-parse optimization, and most of it is genuinely simple: a string test gates a parse that would have produced no diagnostic anyway. What is complected is the relationship between the cheap predicate and the careful parser — they each encode their own notion of 'has named weight', 'has url()', 'has :not(' — and nothing checks they agree. The pattern is also being open-coded five times with subtle differences in boundaries and flags; one named helper would make the shared concept (keyword-set membership over a string) explicit instead of incidental. None of this blocks merge; the import-notation and regex-escaping points are worth tightening before they bite.
